patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/hmm: reject shadow-stack mappings
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch rejects shadow-stack mappings in the Heterogeneous Memory Management (HMM) module to prevent devices from gaining write access to user-space shadow stacks on x86 architectures.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that shadow stack VMAs should be completely disallowed due to security concerns and lack of need for read access, and suggested dropping the existing hmm_range_fault() patch
review_comments.raw_body:
Cool, so I can drop

	e27dc0754e3f4 mm/hmm: refuse shadow stack vmas in hmm_range_fault()

:)

Acked-by: David Hildenbrand (Arm) <david@kernel.org>


I used the comment:

+        * Shadow stack VMAs must not be written, and there is no particular
+        * reason to allow read access to shadow stacks from devices, so just
+        * disallow it entirely.
+        *

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Jason Gunthorpe
review_comments.summary: reviewer questioned why a writable pte for shadow-stack mappings is rejected, noting that only DMA should be restricted from writing to it; he also asked about x86 specifics and suggested adding more explanation
review_comments.raw_body:
I'm not sure I understand this? The pte is writable but you don't want
only DMA to write to it?

Is there something special on x86 that makes the shadow stack pte
non-writable by the CPU?

A few more words here would help

Regardless, this seems reasonable to me, there is no use case to
write to the shadow stack..

Reviewed-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@nvidia.com>

Jason

review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that shadow-stack mappings are technically writable but the kernel should prevent it, agreed to handle the DMA case and is open to a better solution.
review_comments.raw_body:
Some of the context is here:
https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/

We had a similar issue with migration, but this should handle the DMA
case as well.

It's "technically writable" but the kernel is supposed to prevent that.

I will say my understanding of the larger HMM picture is limited, so
there might be a better way than special-casing it like this.

~Gregory

review_comments.author: Jason Gunthorpe
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Jason Gunthorpe noted that pte_write() incorrectly returns true for shadow-stack PTEs, which can lead to devices gaining write access when they shouldn't, and suggested introducing a new function like pte_real_write() to accurately report the write bit.
review_comments.raw_body:
Bah, it's not writable at all. The CPU PTE has write disabled and
someone thought it was a good idea to make pte_write() return true
because the CPU allows writes through a special instruction on this
special PTE? So now all the places like this think its writable, when
it really isn't.

You could also fix this by having something like pte_real_write() or
whatever that doesn't lie about the write bit in the PTE :|

The patch is still fine, in that it matches what everything else does,
but I'd include these details someplace..

Jason

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that on x86, shadow-stack PTEs have their write bit clear but pte_write() reports them writable due to special instructions, allowing GPU access and potential corruption of return addresses or bypassing protection; requested rejecting shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test() including read access
review_comments.raw_body:
How does this look for an altered changelog?

: On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
: rejects ordinary stores to it, but pte_write() reports it writable because
: shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
: HMM_PFN_WRITE, which Nouveau turns into ordinary GPU write permission.  A
: process with GPU access can then overwrite its own shadow stack,
: potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
: 
: Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.  A
: requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledges that shadow-stack mappings should be rejected, but expresses skepticism about the design choice and implies that there may not be an immediate fix.

Author suggests renaming the function pte_write() to pte_fake_write() as an alternative solution, indicating they are open to revising the patch.

Author agrees to adjust the patch changelog as suggested by Jason Gunthorpe, indicating a positive response to feedback.
review_comments.raw_body:
I completely missed this, that will teach me to trust pte_write() I
guess... what a bizarre design choice.  I'm sure there's "reasons".

---

or rename pte_write() to pte_fake_write() instead and restore
pte_write() to its former truthful glory

:| indeed

---

Thank you for taking a closer look, I think Andrew's changelog
adjustment is an improvement if you're ok with it.

-- 
~Gregory

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that pte_write() is sufficient for core-mm's needs, and that nobody besides selected core-mm code should write to random PTEs; they suggested using GUP instead of reimplementing it in HMM
review_comments.raw_body:
It's writable by the hardware, that's what matters to core-mm, for example, when
it comes to things like fork(), mproetect() etc.

*nobody* besides selected core-mm code should ever write to random PTEs. They
shouldn't ever even care about pte_write().

We have GUP for that, which takes care of that oddity properly when deciding
whether we can *actually* write to a mapped page.

Well, and we have HMM that reimplements part of GUP in ugly ways (sorry) that we
missed.

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that on x86, shadow-stack PTEs have their ordinary write bit clear but pte_write() reports them writable due to shadow-stack instructions; this allows HMM to grant devices write access to the process's shadow stack, potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing protection
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks.  This?

On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.

Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

review_comments.author: Jason Gunthorpe
review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a device gains ordinary write access to a shadow stack, which can lead to unexpected behavior

review_comments.author: Alistair Popple
review_comments.summary:
reviewer pointed out that they had previously asked the HMM question on a different thread, and requested clarification on why it was being addressed in this patch

reviewer pointed out that the patch's assumption about shadow-stack mappings being universally writable by HW is incorrect, as _PAGE_RW = 0 and pte_write() returns true for logically writable pages
review_comments.raw_body:
Yeah, I asked the HMM question there -
https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/avT2FNTZoEuijEZP@nvdebian.thelocal/

---

Except they're not universally writable by HW, after all _PAGE_RW = 0. So
pte_write() is documented to return if it is logically writable, which of course
is what hmm_range_fault() also needs for certain values of "logic" :-)

So it's easy to see how this is confusing and got missed. Anyway this fix looks
good:

Reviewed-by: Alistair Popple <apopple@nvidia.com>
